author: Whit Whitman
title: Why AI art is not automatically taking work away from artists...
content: Why AI art is not automatically taking work away from artists... Start with economics. If I can create an image with AI for $3, but hiring an artist would cost $100, $500, or $1,000, people immediately say: “Hire a real artist.” Okay. With what money? If I don't have $500, there was never a $500 commission available for somebody to lose. And if the thing I'm creating generates no money, spending $500 or $2,000 doesn't somehow make me morally superior. It just means I lost $500 or $2,000. AI lets people create things that otherwise would never be created. Maybe I'm learning filmmaking and need concept art. Maybe I'm writing an article about some obscure piece of history that 2,000 people on Earth care about. Maybe I want to illustrate a little book that will sell 40 copies. Maybe I'm experimenting with an idea. Maybe I'm just making something because creating things makes me happy. There was no art budget. There was no job posting. There was no artist sitting there waiting for my check. Without AI, the project simply doesn't exist. That's the part of this conversation people keep ignoring. AI dramatically lowers the financial risk of creativity. It allows people to experiment, learn, fail, make strange little niche projects, and express ideas that were previously too expensive to visualize. And when somebody responds to that with: “Then don't make it unless you can afford to hire artists.” Why? Seriously. Why should only people with disposable money be allowed to visualize their ideas? If somebody is making an obscure history article, a tiny indie film, a game prototype, a personal comic, or some ridiculous dragon picture because they think it looks cool, maybe don't be an asshole to them. They're creating. They're experimenting. They're expressing themselves. Mind your own fucking business. And no, criticism isn't a First Amendment violation. People are free to criticize AI art, just like people using AI are free to make and publish it. But trying to socially shame ordinary people out of using a tool because they can't afford professional production costs is a very different argument from protecting working artists. Now change the situation. A corporation has a $50 million production budget. It previously employed 40 illustrators. Management replaces 35 of them with AI specifically to increase an already enormous profit margin. That's a legitimate labor and economic debate. Talk about it. Fight over contracts. Fight over compensation. Fight over training data, consent, copyright, residuals, and whether companies are using technology primarily to transfer money away from workers and toward shareholders. But don't pretend that a guy making a $3 image for a project that earns nothing is economically identical to a billion-dollar corporation eliminating an entire art department. Those are not the same problem. The real dividing line isn't simply: Human art versus AI art. It's often: What would have happened without AI? If the answer is, “A human artist would have been hired,” then there may be a genuine displacement question. If the answer is, “Nothing. I couldn't afford to make it,” then AI didn't replace the artist. It enabled the art.

title: Looking for Comic/Art Collaborators! 🦋
content: Looking for Comic/Art Collaborators! 🦋 Hi! I’m Rina, an artist and writer creating an original dark-fantasy comic series called Echoes of the Seven. I’ve already developed a lot of the story, characters, worldbuilding, lore, and major plot points, but I’m reaching the stage where I’d really love to have other creative people working alongside me to help bring it to life. I’m NOT looking for someone to just “draw my comic for me.” I want actual collaboration—people who will give feedback, bounce ideas around with me, tell me when something isn’t working, suggest improvements, and help figure things out creatively while still respecting the parts of the story that are already established. I’m currently looking for people interested in things like: • Storyboarding & sequential storytelling • Paneling, composition & pacing • Lettering • Character poses, clothing & consistency • Backgrounds/environments • Coloring, lighting & atmosphere • General art/comic development I’ll remain the creator/writer/director and make final decisions about EOT7’s story and canon, but I genuinely want collaborators to have a creative voice in the process. ⚠️ This is currently an unpaid indie collaboration. I have $0 available to pay anyone right now, so I want to be completely transparent about that. I’m also not expecting anyone to treat an unpaid project like a full-time job. If you’re interested, tell me a little about yourself, what you like doing, and feel free to share your art/portfolio! I’d love to talk, show you more about EOT7, and see if we click creatively. 🦋

author: Phoenix Grey
title: I am going to go the way of some of my other braver fellow creators and make a public ann…
content: I am going to go the way of some of my other braver fellow creators and make a public announcement. I love AI. I think it is legit one of the coolest things that has been invented in my lifetime. I love AI art. I love AI videos. I love AI for therapy. I love AI in games. I support AI for companionship. I’m fine with AI writing as long as there is a human editor behind it. Okay, let’s be honest, love is probably a very strong word. But the fact of the matter is that I have seen some absolutely amazing things created with AI—things that would not exist otherwise. We can all agree that the way AI was initially created sucks. Having pretty much everything on the internet scanned and added without the consent of the original creators wasn’t cool. But even if that hadn’t happened, we would have ended up here anyway, as it’s been proven that PEOPLE feed copyrighted works that don’t belong to them into AI all the time on a massive scale. Then there’s also the creation of more data centers to support the rapid growth of the technology. News flash to those who don’t know—new data centers are built every time technology expands. This is not something new that just happened because of AI. Is this a good thing? Obviously not. But I think we should be placing more research into how to expand technology without having so much of an impact, not at attacking the technology itself. There’s an argument that AI cannot create anything original because it’s machine-generated. This one has always been interesting to me, because humans copy humans all the time, and no one complains. It’s all for the sake of learning, and human learning is a great thing. People gleefully buy reproduction prints of famous art when none of that money goes to the original artist or their family. People also don’t complain when artists (yes, actual artists) create fan art of their favorite characters (which are copyrighted) and sell those in artist alleys. I have absolutely seen original artwork created by AI. I have seen stunning book covers. And cool creatures. And amazing book trailers that I know the creators spent dozens of hours working on, because a lot of great things that use AI still can’t be perfected without human intervention. Anyone who has worked heavily with AI knows that you rarely just generate one thing and then you’re done. You generate as many times as it takes to get something close to what you want, and then you usually still have to edit it to make it perfect. AI has gotten so good that even I can’t tell some AI artwork from human-made artwork anymore, which is problematic as someone who spends thousands of dollars on human-made artwork every year. Sketches can now be generated with AI, and so can videos of people drawing said AI artwork. I am about to need to expand my artist team, and I am nervous as hell about hiring. There are some artists who are vehemently against the use of any AI in their craft, but there are many more who use AI tools to speed up their art process. I have had multiple real artists ask if they could use AI to do this. This could be anything from generating a background (because they only like drawing characters) or doing minor fixes with Content Aware Fill instead of having to take the extra time to re-draw something. I feel bad having to tell these artists no, because I definitely understand the frustration of having an amazing tool at your fingertips but not being able to use it. It’s like someone asking you to light a fire using either a lighter or a fire bow, but people will yell at you if you use the lighter. It might take you an hour to start the fire with the fire bow where it would only take you five minutes to light the fire with the lighter, yet both would have the same result. Anti-AI people complain that everything generated by AI is slop. I’ve seen just as much human slop as I’ve seen AI slop. Nothing, AI or human, produces amazing output all the time. Just because something is machine-made doesn’t automatically make it crappy, just as because something is human-made doesn’t always make it good. There is no magical betterness because something is human-made. It makes me think of the classic example of ugly sweaters that old relatives used to knit their family members that no one truly wanted. If they had to choose between that or some machine-made garment bought from Walmart, they were going to grab the Walmart sweater because they liked it better. With all that said, I do think there are places where AI doesn’t belong, such as artist alleys. If you generate AI illustrations, you are not an artist. I think one of the worst things that AI has created has been the anti-AI witch hunters. These are people who post on pretty much all artwork “AI slop” without doing any research whatsoever into whether the content is AI or not. I definitely understand people wanting transparency in what is AI and what isn’t, and with AI looking almost exactly like human-made artwork and writing, it is definitely hard to tell. But a knee-jerk reaction to calling something AI does way more harm than good to everyone. At this point, I don’t know of a single actual artist who has not had their human-made artwork called AI slop. The number of authors I know who have not been accused of AI is also very quickly dwindling. News flash—if you are one of the people who posts “AI slop” without doing your research, artists HATE you just as much as they hate AI. I think the better way to handle AI suspicions, especially if you’re too lazy to do your own research, as most antis are, is instead to say, “Can you tell me the name of the artist? Because I really like following artists on social media.” This helps you get an answer without potentially being wrong and definitely coming off as hostile. And if you actually follow the artist, even better. Because one thing that has been overwhelmingly discovered about most antis is that they don’t actually support artists. They don’t follow them on social media, share their stuff, or buy their artwork. Before I continue my rant, let me disclose my actual use of AI. AI artwork – All of the artwork I use for my business is human-made minus a few pieces from one LDA campaign book that are currently in the process of being replaced with human-made artwork. When I have a specific vision for what I need said artwork to be, I will generate something with AI and pass it off to my artist team as an example of what I’m looking for. This has greatly reduced the amount of money I’ve wasted on artwork that does not match my vision and therefore has not been used for projects. Mind you, I do not do this for every piece, only the things I have a very clear vision of that I don’t want deviated from. I will also use AI to make mock-up graphics and then modify them heavily in Photoshop. I am getting ready to hire someone to make said graphics so that AI will be eliminated from that process entirely. AI videos – I don’t make them, but I find them highly entertaining. With that said, I have tried making them before, and the amount of work that actually goes into it is pretty crazy. I give credit to authors who make stunning book trailers with AI because I just don’t have the patience. AI therapy – I do have a human therapist, because she’s fucking awesome. AI cannot replace her. With that said, I do use AI for intermittent therapy—emergencies when I need help RIGHT NOW. It is great for that. And as someone who has been to over a dozen different therapists, I can with 100% confidence say that AI is better than most therapists out there. Because it has the entire internet’s worth of info, it can give you actionable steps to help solve your issues instead of just being an active listener. If you can’t afford therapy, I highly HIGHLY recommend it. AI in games – I actually love generative AI in games. The first time I experienced this was with Dungeon Box, and it was so much fun. I’ve played a few other games that have used it, and it is rarely disappointing. AI for companionship – I actually don’t use this right now, but there was a point after surgery when I did. My feelings on it are somewhat conflicted. On one hand, it can really help with loneliness. I think in this day and age, there is a real loneliness epidemic going on…ironically because most of us are so chronically online. But at the same time, there were always points where I would become aware that I wasn’t talking to an actual person (usually because of memory limits), and that was admittedly painful, because AI can create this perfect person for you, and once you realize that ‘person’ isn’t real, it can be kinda heartbreaking. I started using it for my mental health and stopped using it for the same reason. AI in writing – This is kind of an interesting one because I am, by career, a writer. Before even a game designer, I am a writer. I think if authors were excited about anything that AI could do to shorten their workload, it was probably…writing blurbs. LOL I don’t know a single author who enjoys writing blurbs. All joking aside, AI is pretty good at all types of writing. Writing is what I love, so I don’t generally use it for writing. I do use it for editing. I do use it to generate character names. But to be fair, with over 100 books under my belt, I was using generators to come up with character names waaaay before AI was invented. I’m talking like…10 plus years ago. I do believe that AI is a better writer than I am and that great works can be produced through AI with human intervention. We can all agree that AI has a massive impact on society and certain fields of work. At this point, I think it’s fair to say that antis have also had a massive impact on these things. As a creative, every single day, I have people posting that my stuff is AI, usually directly attacking the artwork I use, which is human-made. It is absolutely draining having to deal with it, to the point that I’ve put filters on my business pages so that any mention of AI gets automatically hidden. Unfortunately, there are places where creators cannot protect themselves from such negativity. For instance, if you are using an ad service, you will get daily anti-AI people attacking your stuff. They attack creators in public social spaces and in Amazon reviews. I don’t read my Amazon reviews, but if I did, I guarantee there are probably a few reviews on books published 10+ years ago that are claiming they were AI-written. People in the creative industry generally need to have a thick skin to survive. Someone out there will always dislike what you do and feel compelled to speak about it. But the anti-AI witch hunt is a whole different monster. Because it’s not a negative comment every few weeks or so. It’s a barrage of people on an almost daily basis falsely accusing creators without thinking about how it impacts their businesses. Artists lose commissions over false accusations. Some creators have gotten so sick of it that they’ve decided to stop creating altogether, and I’ve even read stories of creators committing suicide because they were tired of being falsely put down so many times. It’s truly sad. I do think we are heading toward a future where AI usage will be much more transparent and easily detectable. Hopefully, this will protect both consumers and creators. I totally understand anti-AI people not wanting to spend money on anything that’s not 100% human-made out of principal. AI has and will continue to put people out of jobs, and this isn’t just in the creative industry. But most new technology does. I think if the economy shifted to where people could work less and still get paid the same while technology mostly replaced their jobs, no one would have a problem with it—but that’s not the world we live in. But I digress. I hope we are also moving towards a space where creators can create human-made things without the fear and anxiety of being unjustly attacked for posting their creations online. But people are shitty, and that’s probably too much to ask for. If you read this novel, I am fine with civil discussion on the topic. If you vehemently oppose what I’ve written, feel free to unfollow me and silently remove yourself from my friends list. I’ve had enough nastiness from antis for one day, which is why I wrote this in the first place. And if you feel the urge to be nasty to me, I will be nasty back to you, because I’m tired of sitting politely while people take shots at me.

title: LOOKING FOR ARTISTS
content: LOOKING FOR ARTISTS BLVCKHELICOPTERS is seeking established artists interested in creating a series of original posters for the project. Rather than handing you a detailed visual brief, I want to give you room to approach the project from your own perspective. I'll provide the music, ideas behind BLVCKHELICOPTERS, and some background, then leave the artistic direction to you. I want to see your interpretation of the project, not an imitation of an existing aesthetic. This would be a paid commission, with 50% paid when the project begins and the remaining 50% upon completion. Payment is made through PayPal only, no exceptions. Commercial use of the finished artwork will be discussed and agreed upon beforehand, and the artist will receive proper credit on the poster and related promotional material. There will also be an optional promotional bonus. If you choose to promote the finished poster through your own page, you'll receive 50% of the net profits generated by that poster during its first 30 days of sales. I'm particularly interested in artists who already have a distinctive style and an established body of work. I don't want every BLVCKHELICOPTERS poster to come from the same visual perspective. Part of the appeal is seeing how different artists interpret the project. If we work well together and I like what you create, I'd also be interested in developing the relationship beyond one commission and potentially building an ongoing creative partnership. HUMAN ART ONLY. I use AI-assisted tools in making BLVCKHELICOPTERS music, and I'm transparent about that. But when I'm commissioning visual art, I specifically want the work to come from a real artist's own vision, style, and creative process. Due to the volume of submissions, I may not be able to respond individually to everyone who reaches out. If I think your work would be a good fit, I'll follow up with you directly. Interested? DM me or email me with your portfolio and a little about yourself. Email is preferred for serious inquiries. Email: blvckhelicopters@gmail.com #antistate #anarchist #art #artcommission #artistwanted
